title: Slate Electric Truck Orders Officially Open On June 24 And We Should Finally Know What It ...
description:
In addition to standard features not seen in ages like crank windows, Slate has some other bold ideas for this little truck.
Well, color me delightfully surprised: Slate has announced via email to reservation holders that actual pre-orders for the little EV open up on June 24.
Mind you, the one thing we don’t have yet is an actual price for the Slate.
While the marque claimed a starting price under $20,000 with EV rebates, those federal rebates have completely evaporated.
Beyond the bottom line, I’m especially interested in learning what the longer-range model with an estimated 240-ish miles of range costs.
text:
The Slate EV might be the most interesting planned car launch of the year, not because it’s a technological moonshot or a revamp of a wildly successful existing model, but because it’s a litmus test: Are Americans ready for true entry-level EVs? When it was first unveiled last year, it piqued our interests but questions remained around whether it could make it to market. Now it seems to be one big step closer, with actual pre-orders opening soon.

The premise behind the Slate is a rather interesting one: At a time when cars are growing increasingly expensive and DIY-unfriendly, what if someone made an EV in America that did the opposite of those thing? In addition to standard features not seen in ages like crank windows, Slate has some other bold ideas for this little truck. A pair of SUV conversions including curtain airbags that you can supposedly install yourself, a standard battery pack with an estimated range of just 150-ish miles, molded-in-color grey plastic panels instead of paint.

It’s a neat concept and has some serious backing, but I’ll admit, I’ve had my questions about viability. Will Americans be receptive to a short-range EV, even if it’s reasonably cheap? What happens now that federal tax credits have gone away? And will the Slate actually see production? While reservation slots opened at $50 a pop, that sort of thing often doesn’t mean much. I’ve seen plenty of EV efforts fizzle out, and proposed projects get stuck in reservation purgatory. Has anyone seen the second-generation Tesla Roadster recently?

Well, color me delightfully surprised: Slate has announced via email to reservation holders that actual pre-orders for the little EV open up on June 24. To make it into the first delivery window, you’ll have to pay a deposit of $250 if you have a reservation and $300 if you don’t, within 30 days of the portal opening. Otherwise, you’ll simply be bumped down the queue. Slate claims that if you complete that step, they’ll reach out to you as early as this autumn to spec wraps and accessories, finalize the purchase, and arrange delivery. Time flies, right?

Mind you, the one thing we don’t have yet is an actual price for the Slate. While the marque claimed a starting price under $20,000 with EV rebates, those federal rebates have completely evaporated. As such, Slate’s only claiming a base price “in the mid-twenties,” but that’s both subject to change and before any taxes and fees. Is the freight fee factored in there? I haven’t the foggiest, but we should know more come mid-June. Beyond the bottom line, I’m especially interested in learning what the longer-range model with an estimated 240-ish miles of range costs.

Regardless, Slate marching towards production gives me hope. Hope that people still want basic cars. Hope that some automakers are still willing to support DIY maintenance. Hope that North American EVs don’t have to be expensive. It seems like there’s only about a month to go until we learn a whole lot more, so I’m definitely keeping my eyes peeled.

text:
A new 2023 GMC Hummer EV Pickup Edition 1 has surfaced for sale in the Midwest, giving buyers another shot to be the first owner of the first edition of this ambitious EV truck. Listed by Community Buick GMC, the all-electric super truck combines massive power output, advanced off-road capability, and a long list of premium technology features. Finished with the Edition 1 package and equipped with the Extreme Off-Road Package (RPO Z6X), this particular Hummer EV arrives with nearly every major option available from the factory.

The exterior leans heavily into the Hummer EV’s oversized and futuristic design language. Wide fender flares, chunky all-terrain tires, and 18-inch black aluminum wheels with machined accents give the truck a planted stance. This example also includes rocker protectors with assist steps, black rear D-ring recovery hooks, underbody cameras, and a power retractable tonneau cover. GMC’s removable Infinity Roof sky panels (CC3) add an open-air driving experience, while the MultiPro Tailgate Audio System by Kicker turns the tailgate area into a mobile entertainment setup.

Inside, the cabin blends rugged utility with high-end comfort. Heated and ventilated front seats, heated rear seats, and a heated steering wheel come standard on this Edition 1 model. A 13.4-inch GMC Premium Infotainment System with Google built-in handles connectivity duties and supports wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto. Tri-zone automatic climate control, wireless phone charging, Bose Centerpoint 14-speaker audio, and adaptive cruise control further elevate the interior. The Hummer EV also packs a broad suite of driver assistance technologies, including Lane Keep Assist and Enhanced Automatic Parking Assist.

Power comes from GM’s Ultium Drive three-motor electric propulsion system with the 24-module battery pack (ETN), rated at a GM-estimated 1,000 horsepower and 11,500 pound-feet of torque. It’s good for a 0-60 mph time as quick as three seconds in Watts to Freedom (WTF) mode. The setup uses Performance Torque Vectoring e4WD and adaptive air suspension to improve traction and maneuverability on difficult terrain.

The Hummer EV nameplate returned for the 2022 model year under the GMC brand after the original Hummer division shut down in 2010 during GM’s post-bankruptcy restructuring. The Edition 1 served as the launch version of the revived electric truck and quickly sold out following its reveal. Early production models became sought after due to limited availability and the truck’s headline-grabbing performance figures.

Buyers interested in this particular Hummer EV will find it listed with a $20k discount for $94,094 at Community Buick GMC in Waterloo, Iowa. For shoppers seeking a fully loaded electric off-roader with substantial power and unmistakable road presence, this Edition 1 checks nearly every box.

text:
South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster on May 19 signed a bill creating a new state income tax credit that supports the development of landfill gas-to-renewable natural gas (RNG) projects within the state.

The bill, SB 556, allows eligible taxpayers to claim an income tax credit of 25% of the costs incurred for the purchase and installation of equipment used to produce RNG for commercial purposes, with a cap of $5 million per year per taxpayer. Expenses related to offsite utility infrastructure, land acquisition costs, legal expenses, administrative costs and unrelated pipeline expansion are not eligible for the credit.

The tax credit is nonrefundable but can be carried forward up to 15 years for credits earned before 2030. The credit may also be transferred to another eligible taxpayer. The credit is currently in place for tax years beginning after 2025 and ending before taxable year 2030. If a regulated utility receives the credit, it must pass the benefit on to ratepayers.

text:
The Detroit Regional Chamber's policy conference on Mackinac Island is happening this week, bringing together politicians and government officials with businessmen.

The first two days were busy day at the policy conference, from sessions to a bill signing, but one issue on everyone's mind: data centers.

"This is fundamental infrastructure, but it has to be deployed and it has to be executed with community and citizen first," Glenn Stevens, Jr., Chief Automotive and Innovation Officer at the Detroit Regional Chamber, said.

Politics: Mackinac Island ferry fees, rising visitor costs discussed at policy conference

At least three panels focused on artificial intelligence and data centers, including one featuring former Michigan Governor and U.S. Energy Secretary Jennifer Granholm.

"Folks are wondering, 'am I going to have to foot the bill for these data centers?'" Granholm said.

Granholm looked at the issue from the energy perspective, saying data centers can actually lower costs, if they're done right.

"I say that because they're paying for a lot of the infrastructure, the upgrades, etc., if they're required to, they and many of them, like Google, has raised their hand and said, we're going to do that," she said.

Granholm says those upgrades take the onus off of ratepayers.

Liz Schwab, head of data center market development and policy for Google, agreed, noting the role they play in an ever-digital world.

"We have this new vector of demand called AI. I saw a report out this week, the average weekly usage amongst U.S. Adults in February was about 43% and this month it jumped up to 65%," Schwab said. "So folks are starting to use agents and AI more regularly in their daily lives, and of course, we've got a we've got a bill to support that as well."

Schwab, however, said she understands public apprehension.

Still, she said there are misconceptions about noise, water and energy use, especially since they get state tax incentives.

"We have to certify 90% clean energy procurement. We have to ensure ratepayer protections, through, you know, not not using any special utility tariffs, which again goes in front of the MPSC (Michigan Public Service Commission), so that's a very public process," Schwab said. "We have to use municipal water and ensure ahead of time that that municipal water utility has the capacity to serve us."

The panel, though, conceded information sharing needs to be improved.

Politics: Governor Gretchen Whitmer says she won't run for president in 2028

Elected officials, for their part, took a more cautious tone.

"It's the 10 million people in this state who are going to save this state, and I'm excited to have the opportunity to lead them forward into the future," Rep. John James,(R), candidate for governor, said. "As far as data centers are concerned, look, we have to diversify our economy, but it cannot be at the expense of those 10 million people. Michigan is open for business, but we are not for sale."

The conversation continues, as will happen with each issue at the conference.

text:
By Nora Caley

From the May/June 2026 Issue

Despite economic uncertainty, the automotive industry continues to roll along. In an environment of rising fuel prices, high interest rates, and low consumer confidence, auto sales remain resilient. Manufacturers are increasing efficiencies, speeding innovation, and communicating the latest gadgetry and style options.

According to the National Automotive Dealers Association (NADA), the sales for new light-vehicle totaled 16.2 million units in 2025, an increase of 2.4% compared to 2024. Economic headwinds might have encouraged some of those sales. NADA reported that tariff announcements induced some consumers to buy a vehicle before the those took effect.

A similar phenomenon happened with the September 30, 2025 expiration of federal electric vehicle tax credits. Buying activity increased in third quarter, leading to a record-high monthly market share for battery electric vehicles (BEV) of 11.8%. For all of 2025, NADA reported, sales of EVs totaled 1.26 million units, an increase of 1.2% compared to 2024.

Even without the federal tax credit, shoppers are interested in EVs. According to the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, in fourth quarter 2025, EVs represented 9.6% of new light-duty vehicle sales. While that was down from 10.2% in 2024, there are still 164 models of electric car, utility vehicle, pickup truck and vans now available for sale in the U.S. (For another perspective on EV sales during 2025, see the sidebar on page 48.)

Whether they are building EVs or gasoline-powered vehicles, automotive businesses employed 952,800 workers in March 2026, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. While that was down from 975.3 in March 2025, the industry remains a robust employer.

Companies continue to look for sites to build state-of-the-art facilities, and locations are heralding their advantages. Following are some locations that are attracting the interest of automotive manufacturers and suppliers.

Gadsden, Alabama: Dynamic Automotive Manufacturing

Nestled in the foothills of Northeast Alabama, Etowah County has quietly become one of the most dynamic automotive manufacturing communities in the American South. Home to multiple Tier 1 and Tier 2 automotive suppliers, including the Narmco Group, Inteva Products, and Fehrer Automotive, the county has built a supply chain ecosystem that serves some of the world’s largest automakers.

Geography has played a decisive role in shaping this ecosystem. Gadsden, the county seat, sits within a two-hour drive of six major OEMs: Honda, Mercedes, Volkswagen, Toyota, Hyundai, and Mazda-Toyota, placing local suppliers squarely at the center of the Southeast’s automotive corridor. The county is further connected by Interstate 59, Norfolk Southern rail to the Port of Mobile, and the Northeast Alabama Regional Airport, with Birmingham-Shuttlesworth International Airport 60 minutes away, Huntsville International Airport 90 minutes away, and Atlanta’s Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport within two hours. Being in the center of these logistical hubs, Etowah County is equally effective for domestic distribution and global supply chain connectivity.

In early 2026, that connectivity drew one of the region’s most significant investments in a generation. Global automotive supplier Minth Group Limited announced plans to invest $430 million and create more than 1,300 jobs at the former Gulf States Steel site in Gadsden, a 400-acre brownfield that had long symbolized the region’s industrial past. The facility will encompass nearly one million square feet of manufacturing space and produce high-quality plastic and aluminum components for automakers’ North American plants. The Taiwan-based company, which operates 78 plants globally, selected Gadsden as its flagship U.S. campus, citing the region’s workforce, infrastructure, and proximity to major OEMs.

The appeal of Etowah County to automotive manufacturers is no accident. “People here know how to work,” said David Hooks, Executive Director of the Gadsden-Etowah Industrial Development Authority. “They appreciate the opportunity to work. They expect to be paid for it, but they don’t mind working.”

That culture of craftsmanship and reliability is supported by more than 500,000 residents within a 60-mile radius of Gadsden, providing a deep, experienced labor pool. Gadsden State Community College’s newly opened 50,000-square-foot Advanced Manufacturing Center reinforces that pipeline, offering immersive training in mechatronics, precision machining, and additive manufacturing; skills that translate directly to the automotive industry.

For companies evaluating expansion, the county offers industrial sites at every scale. The 1,250-acre Northeast Alabama Regional (NEAR) Megasite, featuring a 100-acre shovel-ready pad, an on-site power substation, a 500,000-gallon water tank, and direct rail access, is designed to help large-scale manufacturers begin production quickly. The 25-acre Airport Industrial Park, an Alabama AdvantageSite, offers suppliers and logistics operations a streamlined, smaller footprint. All sites carry the infrastructure readiness and certified status that global site selectors demand.

What Minth Group recognized, and what Etowah County’s growing roster of automotive suppliers already knows, is that the community offers a place where infrastructure, workforce, and regional collaboration are priorities.

Visit gadsdenida.org for more information.

text:
A top state Senate Republican is criticizing Democrats for “anti-business” policies that he believes led to oil giant ExxonMobil choosing to redomicile in Texas.

The oil giant is reincorporating in Texas, where the company is headquartered and where most of the company’s U.S. operations are conducted. ExxonMobil’s shareholders approved the move Wednesday.

But Senate Minority Leader Anthony M. Bucco is criticizing state Democrats for ignoring “warning signs” that the state has become inhospitable to major businesses.

“ExxonMobil’s decision to leave New Jersey for Texas should be a wake-up call for every elected official in Trenton,” Bucco said. “After more than a century tied to our state, one of the world’s largest companies is telling New Jersey what many others have already made clear: the business climate has become too expensive, overregulated, and hostile to employers.”

ExxonMobil had been headquartered in Spring, Texas, since 1989, but the company had remained incorporated in New Jersey. ExxonMobil leaders said reincorporating in Texas makes logistical sense for the company, and said Texas’s “legal and regulatory environment,” including a special court tasked with resolving complex business disputes, influenced the move.

“Over the past several years, Texas has made a noticeable effort to embrace the business community. In doing so, it has created a policy and regulatory environment that can allow the company to maximize shareholder value,” said Darren Woods, ExxonMobil chairman and CEO. “Aligning our legal home with our operating home, in a state that understands our business and has a stake in the company’s success, is important.”

ExxonMobil is the latest major company to reincorporate in Texas, which last year passed legislation making the state’s legal system friendlier to corporations.

Bucco pointed to the closure of the Anheuser-Busch brewery in Newark and Johnson & Johnson’s decision to open a $1 billion facility in Pennsylvania as evidence of New Jersey’s business-hostile system.

“New Jersey already has some of the highest business taxes in the nation, yet Democrats keep doubling down on policies that make it harder to operate here,” Bucco said. “Families and workers ultimately pay the price when companies leave, jobs disappear, and investment dries up.”

text:
Canada’s biofuels sector is at a pivotal moment as industry leaders warn that delays and uncertainty around Clean Fuel Regulations (CFR) amendments could stall investment and shift production opportunities south of the border.

In this Canadian Agri-Food Policy Institute (CAPI) webinar presented in partnership with RealAgriculture and BASF Agricultural Solutions, panellists from across the fuel, grain, ethanol, and oilseed processing sectors discussed the growing pressure to align Canadian policy with the U.S. Inflation Reduction Act’s 45Z clean fuel production tax credit.

David Schick, vice-president for western Canada, innovation and regulatory affairs with the Canadian Fuels Association, said biofuels are now viewed as essential to maintaining refinery competitiveness and ensuring long-term energy security. “We’re going to need these liquid fuels and we need to make sure we’re evolving them,” Schick said, pointing to aviation, rail, agriculture, and heavy-duty transportation as sectors that will continue to rely on liquid fuels for decades.

Several of the speakers stress that Canada risks losing investment without policy certainty. Andrea Kent, vice-president of government and industry affairs with Greenfield Global, said the ethanol sector is already feeling the impact of heavily subsidized U.S. imports. “The threat has already arrived,” Kent said, warning that stalled expansion projects and delayed investments could eventually lead to plant closures if Canadian producers remain at a disadvantage.

For canola growers, the discussion centred on domestic demand growth and market diversification. Brittany Wood, senior manager of transportation and trade policy with the Canadian Canola Growers Association, said Canadian biofuel production has already added roughly 500,000 tonnes of domestic canola oil consumption since the CFR was introduced.

Chris Vervaet, senior associate with Bjornson and Associates and former executive director of the Canadian Oilseed Processors Association, highlighted how renewable diesel demand has doubled over the past five years, driving major canola crush expansion across Western Canada. He noted that by the end of this year, Canada’s crush capacity is expected to reach 15 million tonnes annually — roughly 75 per cent of Canadian canola production.

It's clear that biofuels are no longer just a climate policy discussion, but increasingly tied to trade, energy security, rural investment, and long-term agricultural competitiveness in North America.

Our theme this year is Canadian Agri-Food in a Value-Added World. First and foremost, register before the 15th of June to take advantage of our launch pricing and save on the registration costs. But really, we all think that this discussion today on biofuels is a great example of this value-added world that we're in and the need to better understand what are the pressures, what are the opportunities, what are the challenges that we face, and how can we do a better job taking the production that we have in Canada and adding more value to it. And so with that, let's take a look at the poll results and see what you had to tell us today. And so we've got kind of a split here. We've got a mix of people saying market integration, trade dynamics, industrial competitiveness, fuel affordability, and climate. And so clearly there is a set of issues that you think are going to be pressures today, and we will wait and see what our panellists have to say about that. And so over to you then, Shaun, to help kick things off and get the in-depth discussion going. Hey, appreciate it, Tyler. Great stuff. And you can definitely see the split there across those results. Indeed. What we're going to do is we're going to have a one-on-one conversation here with David Schick. He is with the Canadian Fuels Association and with the CFA, this version of the CFA. Yeah, thanks, Shaun. Thanks for including me. Yeah. Okay. So I guess off the top, who does the Canadian Fuels Association represent? Who are your members? Our members are the folks that produce and distribute transportation fuels in Canada. So you have to have operations in Canada to be a member. So these are integrated oil companies, but also the renewable fuel suppliers and increasingly traditional oil gas companies are producing their own renewable fuels within their operations. So those are the folks we represent. So 96% of the fuel that's distributed in Canada are our members. And I guess, would you consider the Canadian fuels industry to be— are you— would you classify yourself as pro-biofuel? And I guess answer that one first. Yeah, well, I would actually. I think that it's pretty clear to us that if you're going to evolve the transportation fuel sector and you understand that there's going to be a need for liquid fuels, biofuels is going to be a big part of that. And it became apparent to me a number of years ago that if you want to maintain your refineries' competitiveness in a way the globe is moving towards lower carbon fuels, you need to integrate biofuels into that process, not just in blending, but also manufacturing them through our existing processes in order to sort of ensure we can maintain the utilisation of those facilities and make sure that they're lower carbon for the future. Was it always this way? Where was the— was the association and its members always pro-biofuel? No, we were the Canadian Petroleum Products Institute in 2012. And that sounds very anti-biofuel, Dave. Yeah, I know it was. Well, when I started all of this, I used to go to the renewable fuels conferences and hear fire and brimstone storeys about how the oil and gas industry was the most wicked thing in the world. And then those folks would step off the stage and ask me if I wanted to buy some ethanol. So I think it's a real— that was sort of the lead-in to where we got to. And what happened, I think, is that the previous Liberal government was focused on electrification. And so the folks that made liquid fuels and understood we were going to need them for a long time started to realise we had more in common than apart. And so we started to work more closely together with agriculture and with the biofuels standalone facilities, acknowledging that we were going to need, especially in Canada, given our, our expansive geography, we're going to need these liquid fuels and we need to make sure we're evolving them. So that changed in the last 3 or 4 years. Okay. So it is rather recent then. That's okay. That is interesting. Now, currently there's a lot of push from your members as well as the agricultural industry to make some changes to the Clean Fuel Regulation. And you'll hear it throughout the webinar today referred to as the CFR amendment. What is the single most critical change that the CFA would like to see with those amendments? Well, we'd like to see competitiveness in terms of the incentive structures with the US IRA 45Z. And what that means is that historically there's been a blender's tax credit in the states. They move to this thing that we talk about in our sector all the time, which is a production tax credit. And so the US has this significant incentive, a subsidisation of their facilities and when they sell the product into Canada, they get all the Canadian credits and stuff from the CFR. So this puts our, our producing people in Canada at a significant disadvantage. So the CFR amendments as outlined have a couple of things that we're looking for. The main one is a multiplier on the number of credits, which directly offsets, to avoid trade issues, directly offsets the 45Z to help us get to a level playing field, and, and that's the main thing that we're looking for. Now, is that the case for both ethanol and renewable diesel, or are there differences between the two of those in those amendment changes? The numbers can change. I think it's true for both. We're seeing some stuff on the ethanol side that's of concern where there's tax credits for carbon sequestration, which lowers the carbon intensity of the fuel. That's the currency of how we measure these things. It's not just volumes of products. It's the lower carbon intensity has a bigger impact. And now you can produce your credits. So there's a major pipeline for ethanol plants being put in to sequester the carbon, and that's going to lower their carbon intensity, which could really be a challenge to our ethanol producers in Canada. And on both bio-based diesel, we call it, which is renewable diesel and biodiesel, we're importing about 60% there and in ethanol from the US. And given all of the foundational pieces we have in Canada to do a good job of making these things here, That's a problem increasingly on energy supply reliability, on making sure we can do it and maintaining our sovereignty. Given we have that vulnerability, we're open, we want free trade, but we just want to make sure that Canada's producing in an optimal way to support our domestic market as well as look towards exportation in the future. Yeah, in order for the IRA to not be a threat, we need to find a way for the CFR and the IRA to be somewhat complementary to each other. Is that, is that fair? Yeah, complementary or sort of equitable, I think, is what it boils down to. What we've seen is a tremendous amount of, like, we call it an incentive stack. So where you get benefit from certain policies and credit generation. For instance, in British Columbia, as a more rigorous programme than the federal program, we had a flood of renewable diesel into that market over the last number of years. And in 2024, we're up to 31% renewable content in diesel. But very little of that was produced in Canada, and that's slowly changing. But it is a significant opportunity that's lost and, and actually to the benefit of agriculture, which can be a highly supportive outlet for product and reduces geopolitical risk. I think that's one of the great things for agriculture. And over the next decade or two, also forestry residues can be turned into liquids that we can make fuel out of. And that process is commercialising now, but not at scale. The big deal is canola. We have a lot of it and the energy industry uses a lot of product. And that's really one of the global sort of benefits in Canada is we have a lot of this product that could potentially be used for making, making these renewable fuels. Yeah. Now, are there some administrative bottlenecks and delays regarding the the carbon intensity approvals that, you know, are really kind of this currency, as you discussed, that are slowing down some of your refineries here in Canada? Yeah, it's been a challenge. And I think that, you know, one of the things that we're dealing with is a regulatory structure that the CFR was put under, which is the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, has a lot of rigidity in it because it's a pollution pass-go type regulation where you can't buy your way out. You have to be very— as one would expect. Well, now we have the CFR, which is fundamentally a market-driven thing that has a bunch of different variables and a bunch of different ways you can comply. And yet the rigour necessitated by UCCC because of that structure makes it difficult to get the information. And also from foreign suppliers, you have to gather all that stuff and then it needs to be third-party verified. We'd like to see that sped up significantly. It would be a big help to us. But, you know, the Canadian Environmental Protection Act as obligated parties, which our members are, and to meet these targets is a criminal statute. So that's when we're conservative about things we ask for and try to get flexibility. It's because partially because of that. Now, you mentioned this earlier, the idea of liquid biofuels kind of being skipped, going from petroleum-based fuel all the way to electrification. I guess talk about the necessity for liquid biofuels here in terms of being more of a permanent, a permanent place as opposed to just sort of this temporary bridge that people have been trying to skip. For sure. I mean, we identified it pretty early on that we weren't going to be able to electrify everything. And I think that, you know, it doesn't mean electrification isn't going to play a prominent role, but we have what we refer to as the hard-to-decarbonize sectors. And those, we're going to need liquid fuels for a long time because they need to be highly intense or dense in terms of their BTUs, you know, how much energy is there. And they have to be able to be moved around very easily. So this is aviation, rail, long-haul transportation. Agriculture is another one because it's hard to imagine us being able to have electricity at the volumes that we need, where we need them all the time. For our industrial sectors and for transportation, given the scale of the country. And that further has been sort of shown up because now we're looking at further requirements on the grid like AI, like all of the different things that we're looking for on our making sure our homes are, are less energy intensive. And so for transportation fuels, I think electrification can play an important role in light duty vehicles in urban areas. It can play an important role for return to base deliveries and buses and that kind of thing. But as we expand, given the scale of the country, there really isn't a practical technology to keep medium and heavy-duty vehicles, planes and stuff moving around without liquids. And we can lower the carbon intensity to very low levels now. We see pathways forward. So the liquid fuels can be a really powerful way to have good carbon outcomes. And not put unnecessary strain on the grid. I'm curious, from your perspective at the Canadian Fuels Association, how can your group work more collaboratively with the biofuel sector and the agricultural industry? If you want to look at it as a three-legged stool, there's probably some legs there I'm missing, but are there opportunities to be a little bit more collaborative on this file? Absolutely there is. I think that You know, I think we lost the plot over the last few years a little bit. When we started talking about renewable fuels policies, as they started in the States, started with the farmers, and it was a way to make sure that they were supporting their market. And then there was a benefit of, of improvement to the environment. Our previous government extended that, made it more difficult and more dense around decarbonization was the only thing we were talking about, forgetting about affordability, reliability, supply, all the other critical things that we need. And so I think what we need to do between agriculture and the energy industry is to describe to those that are pushing back against the opportunities for biofuels from economic growth, for rural development, supporting and diversifying our markets. That storey needs to be told along with decarbonization so that it becomes a bipartisan thing in Canada where the federal Conservatives and, or the Conservatives and the Liberal mindset, our understanding that this is good for the country. And I think that we can work— working with agriculture and energy together, two of the largest sectors in our economy, that would— that's an opportunity set for us. Yeah. We think that it's exceptionally well-timed, especially with a focus on renewable fuels and biofuels that they've given it. I think getting leadership both at the federal and the provincial levels back in lockstep is important, not just when you look at kind of that used to kind of be part of the biofuels broader sectoral storey in Canada pre-CFR, but also just looking at successful, you know, kind of sectors who have been able to advance their own industries and their own opportunities as part of this trade negotiation, you need to have that provincial backup with you. So, you know, certainly looking at ethanol, working with Ontario, as Bruce mentioned, that's a province that's already kind of stepped up, right? Saw the cannoli in the, the canary in the mine and, you know, kind of did something as an interim to 45C. Quebec is another, you know, kind of just wealth of production and growers for us. So hopefully that FPT comes out with a report that is very, very, you know, kind of solid on biofuels production and growth and investment oriented, helps us solidify the farm to fuel kind of ag to energy corridor, right? Because no department can kind of do that on their own. I think NRCan, Natural Resources, is well suited to do it and also makes it public so we can all read their good work, right? Great, thank you. So let's go around the table one last time. I'll use a question from Cammie that was in the chat to wrap things up with everyone, and Bruce, we'll go to you first on this. What's the single most important policy signal Canada needs to send right now to keep biofuel investment anchored here rather than shifting to the US? So we'll go to Bruce, then Brittany. Well, I think we've kind of answered that in terms of continuing to you know, do create those, that mechanism that is going to drive demand. And I think the US sort of relationship right now is critical from a signal perspective. We're going to be down as part of a mission next week in Washington. You know, we'll be arguing and supporting this concept of an integrated, you know, North American marketplace. We argued something very similarly on the marine side a year ago and won. We went further to say this was a fortress North American approach and the Americans bought in. But so, you know, I think that's going to be an important signal in general, right, that we'll see from cross-border negotiations and discussions which are about to kick off. Okay, thanks, Bruce. Brittany, to you, one signal that governments can send? I think it's integrating North American feedstock into these targeted amendments, ensuring that North American feedstock book are required in order to, yeah, have any of these additional supports like the credit multiplier or minimum domestic content, etc., that are put forward. So that's what we want to see, and that will drive real incremental growth for canola demand and biofuels in Canada. Thanks. Chris, to you. Make it nonpartisan, and if I can add one more, extend the ambition beyond 2030. Make it longer term. Great, thank you. And Andrea, to you, the final word. CFR and trade are both going to be way less durable and way more difficult for all of us if they do not unlock investment and they do not create stability for farmers, right? So I would say, much like the biofuels incentive for renewable diesel and canola that came out in September, ethanol has not received a signal that Canada will invest in ethanol production yet. So whether it is part of the CFR amendment process, whether it is something announced as part of the FPT or beforehand, put in an ethanol-specific credit multiplier now, tell corn farmers that they can exhale a little bit, and then we can all contribute more broadly and more constructively to things that are longer term like the CFR and to Canada-US trade negotiations for generations to come. Great, thank you, Andrea, Chris, Bruce, Brittany, and to Dave before. Shaun, I will hand it over to you to wrap things up and to sign off. Great stuff. Well, you know, Tyler, I think this has been really awesome because I think this is a topic that does need more attention. And there's— it's not just attention, but there's things to be done. Right? We've got to move. We saw it in the chat. We got to move faster. We have, especially from an ethanol perspective, we have CFR amendments that are being suggested and pushed by not only the fuels industry, but also agriculture and everyone in between to, as a defence mechanism against our entire industry really being challenged from a survivability standpoint. We want to avoid the outcome that the UK has experienced. And on the renewable diesel side, it's a tremendous opportunity. And the delegation that's going down to DC next week, you know, I really hope, Tyler, that they are talking about how Canadian feedstock, specifically canola, lead to not only fuel security but also affordability for American taxpayers, as affordability is just as big of a concern in the US as it is in Canada. So this is really a you know, if you were to go back 10 years, there's kind of a policy that was sort of talked about in some corners of some meetings, but does not necessarily have the full frontal focus that it does now. So I appreciate all of our guests joining us here today. It's been awesome. I learned a lot. It's great. Yeah, great. And again, this is what we're here for, Shaun, is to shine some of that light. So appreciate the partnership with RealAg on this. And we also want to acknowledge and appreciate the support from BASF. And their ongoing support and leadership in this too. Stay tuned to CAPI and RealAgriculture for what comes next. Thank you very much, everyone, for joining us.

text:
POET, a South Dakota-headquartered company and the world’s largest producer of biofuels, has joined with Antora Energy to commission a 5-GWh, multi-day thermal energy storage system at POET’s bioprocessing facility in Big Stone City, South Dakota.

Antora is supplying batteries from the company’s recently expanded San Jose, California gigafactory. The companies earlier in May said the project, which supplies power for POET’s biofuel production, was completed in less than 12 months. The groups said it will be fully operational later this year, and noted it will rank among the world’s largest energy storage installations.

The companies said the project uses Antora’s technology to improve efficiency and lower costs at POET Bioprocessing-Big Stone. The groups did not provide the size of the investment for the project, but did say it has created and supported more than 300 manufacturing and construction jobs in rural South Dakota. It also provided jobs at Antora’s San Jose factory, where all of the company’s thermal batteries are made.

Offtake Agreement

Antora’s system provides POET with 24/7 energy under a long-term heat offtake agreement. It enables the facility to increase bioethanol production, which primarily benefits farmers in South Dakota.

“POET is dedicated to supplying the world with affordable, American-made biofuels and bioproducts,” said Jeff Broin, POET founder and CEO. “Our nation’s energy future will be defined by innovation, and that’s exactly what we’re focused on—pushing the boundaries of what’s possible and delivering viable solutions that strengthen national security and rural economies. By investing in next-generation technologies, we’re leading the way to a biofuture powered by American energy.”

“With this project, Antora is delivering affordable energy to POET—fast,” said Andrew Ponec, co-founder and CEO of Antora Energy. “We’re proud of what this deployment means for the workers who designed, built, and installed these batteries, and more broadly, for American manufacturing. This is what reindustrialization looks like— American innovation driving industrial competitiveness, domestic supply chains spanning a dozen states, and jobs from the factory floor to the construction site. And it’s all delivered at the speed required to meet soaring domestic energy demand.”

John Thune, a U.S. senator for South Dakota, said, “Homegrown energy sources create good-paying jobs, support our agriculture producers, and provide affordable options for consumers. I’m grateful for this impressive addition to South Dakota’s budding biofuels industry, and I can’t wait to see the benefits for South Dakota producers and families across our state.”

The companies said that Grok Ventures, an Australian investment firm, structured and provided the project-level financing as the sole external investor.

“Antora has built something genuinely compelling, a technology and a team capable of delivering affordable, reliable energy to American industry at real scale,” said Ridhaa Ahmed, head of Infrastructure and Private Equity at Grok Ventures. “Our conviction in the technology, the team, and the commercial fundamentals gave us the confidence to structure a financing solution befitting the project’s transformative nature. The commercial logic is strong, the opportunity consequential, and we look forward to continuing our partnership with Antora as they scale this technology across America and the world.”

The South Dakota Board of Economic Development is a partner in the project. Antora’s technology has received funding for research and development from the U.S. Dept. of Energy.

Antora said it worked closely with Otter Tail Power—a Minnesota-headquartered utility that provides power to customers across South Dakota, North Dakota, and Minnesota—to develop an innovative electric rate that enables the system to deliver 24/7 thermal energy without increasing costs for other electricity consumers. The rate structure was approved by the South Dakota Public Utilities Commission last year.

“What we’ve built in South Dakota shows Antora can deliver the reliable and affordable energy required for American competitiveness,” said Jordan Kearns, executive vice president of Project Development at Antora Energy. “We’re proud of what we’ve built with POET, and we’re ready to bring our solution to industrial facilities and data centers across America.”

title: Changes to New Source Review Program Would Mean Higher Costs, Health Risks | EDF
description:
EPA has proposed changing part of the Clean Air Act’s New Source Review program to allow construction to begin on new, large sources of industrial pollution without Congressionally required protections for people nearby.
EPA’s New Source Review program also requires that communities be notified and allowed to comment before a permit is issued.
The Trump EPA is now claiming that weakening New Source Review is necessary to allow for economic growth, but Sarang’s testimony includes evidence of robust economic growth for more than 40 years while the program has been in place and protecting American communities.
EPA’s proposal also singles out Artificial Intelligence (AI) infrastructure and power generation to support data centers as beneficiaries of this policy change, which Sarang discusses in her testimony.
“Contrary to EPA’s assertions, this policy will in fact stymie — not support — the development of affordable power for American families,” says Sarang.
text:
(Washington, D.C. – May 28, 2026) An Environmental Defense Fund expert joined dozens of other Americans at an EPA hearing today to oppose a policy change that could increase costs and health risks for people across the country.

EPA has proposed changing part of the Clean Air Act’s New Source Review program to allow construction to begin on new, large sources of industrial pollution without Congressionally required protections for people nearby.

“Congress ensured that decisions about the location and construction of new industrial sources of pollution are made only after consideration of air quality and environmental impacts and with input from the affected community,” said EDF Senior Attorney Surbhi Sarang in her testimony today. “EPA’s proposal to allow owners and operators to begin construction before a New Source Review permit is issued — and before there has been any consideration of impacts to local air quality, alternatives, or control technologies — unlawfully undermines this intent.”

The Clean Air Act’s New Source Review program requires a permit for any construction, operation, or modification of major sources of industrial pollution. The permits are not issued without first examining the impact on local air quality, and in areas of nonattainment with EPA’s health-based National Ambient Air Quality Standards without first considering potential alternative sites and determining whether the benefits of the facility outweigh the environmental and social costs of its location, construction, or modification. EPA’s New Source Review program also requires that communities be notified and allowed to comment before a permit is issued.

The Trump EPA is now claiming that weakening New Source Review is necessary to allow for economic growth, but Sarang’s testimony includes evidence of robust economic growth for more than 40 years while the program has been in place and protecting American communities. EPA’s proposal also singles out Artificial Intelligence (AI) infrastructure and power generation to support data centers as beneficiaries of this policy change, which Sarang discusses in her testimony.

“Contrary to EPA’s assertions, this policy will in fact stymie — not support — the development of affordable power for American families,” says Sarang. “Reducing review of new fossil fuel power plants to support data centers and AI increases the risk of saddling American families with higher healthcare costs and energy bills and reduces transparency for which the American public is overwhelmingly asking … EPA’s proposal is contrary to the text and purpose of the Clean Air Act and would result in financial and health costs for communities across the country. EDF strongly opposes the proposal and urges EPA to withdraw it.”

text:
A $30 million grant from the Federal Aviation Administration will be used by St. Louis Lambert International Airport to help pay for the construction of a modernized electricity facility that’s central to the airport's plan to consolidate its two terminals into one.

The grant, which was lauded by public officials on Thursday, will be combined with another $20 million awarded last year for the project.

“It’s what will keep this airport running on a daily basis, keep everything alive, keep all the generators running and also be able to ensure that we’ve got the resilience that we currently have concerns about,” Lambert Director Rhonda Hamm-Niebruegge said.

The renovation of what is known as the central utility plant, which was originally built in 1956, and a new Ameren substation will cost roughly $200 million. The remainder of the project not covered by the federal grants will be paid with bonds issued by Lambert.

Republican Sen. Eric Schmitt and Democratic Rep. Wesley Bell, who both advocated for the FAA grant, described the modernized terminal as needed for the region.

“Not only does it have to do with the future prosperity of this region, it also has to do with the self-esteem of the region,” Schmitt said. “This is a great place in our country, a great American city, a region that has a lot to be proud of and deserves an airport that gets us from here to there that is a showcase for this great part of the country.”

With an improved airport, the federal lawmakers and other regional officials also believe the St. Louis region will be more competitive for businesses to move into the region or expand current operations.

“When companies decide where to expand and create job hubs, the status of the airport is one of the first things that they look at,” Bell said. “Too often, Lambert's aging infrastructure has been a factor in St. Louis becoming excluded from those conversations. This federal investment helps make St. Louis more competitive by improving and expanding the airport.”

It’s expected the consolidated terminal, which would branch out of the existing first terminal, would first open in phases by 2028 and would be complete by 2032. The single terminal would consist of 62 gates, expanded concessions, improved roadways and a new parking garage.

The airlines that operate out of Lambert and will largely finance the consolidation have approved the preparation work for the project and roughly 30% of the design. They are expected to give their final decision on the whole project next fall when the design stage will reach 60% completion and a firm price tag will be set.

When introduced in 2022, Lambert officials anticipated the consolidation to cost between $2.8 billion and $3 billion, but that’s expected to increase due to inflation and higher costs for labor and materials.

Eventually, the area officials are hopeful Lambert can one day return to its hub status that it held until the 2000s after American Airlines bought Trans World Airlines.

Hamm-Niebruegge, who’s retiring this fall after leading the airport for 16 years, believes it would take population growth in the area to persuade an airline to make Lambert a hub like those in Chicago, Dallas, New York, Philadelphia or Atlanta.

“They're seeing continued growth in some of those regions, which is important to the airlines to know not only the local numbers there, but, as we bring connecting traffic through, those costs can be viable,” Hamm-Niebruegge said.

Mayor Cara Spencer said the FAA’s decision to award Lambert the grant is “a vote of confidence” in the airport’s future.

“You can count on the City of St. Louis to be a continued partner in this work — regardless of political lines, regardless of other factionalization that has occurred from time to time in the political landscape,” Spencer said. “We are here to do this work together.”

text:
A bill aimed at making Louisiana more enticing to the wood pellet industry has sailed through the state Legislature.

House Bill 670 won unanimous approval in the Louisiana House and Senate and was granted final passage on Wednesday (May 27). It would ease regulations for pellet manufacturers while directing state support toward workforce development, financial incentives and infrastructure improvements designed to meet the industry’s needs.

The industry has come under fire for repeatedly breaking air pollution rules in Louisiana and Mississippi and contributing to greenhouse gas emissions in the United Kingdom, where most of the pellets are burned to produce energy marketed as “sustainable biomass.”

The bill’s supporters admitted they knew little about the industry but backed the measure in hopes of reviving the state’s struggling logging sector.

“This is an opportunity we have in Louisiana that we should capitalize on,” said Rep. Chuck Owen, a Republican from Vernon Parish and the bill’s sponsor.

Owen said he was unfamiliar with pellet manufacturing before industry representatives approached him about drafting the legislation. He repeatedly failed to answer basic questions from his colleagues about where and how the pellets are produced.

Despite this confusion and little discussion about the industry’s lengthy record of violating pollution regulations, the bill moved quickly through the Legislature and is now expected to be signed into law by Gov. Jeff Landry, who has backed similar measures aimed at boosting industrial growth in Louisiana.

British energy company Drax operates Louisiana’s two large wood pellet mills, located near Urania in central Louisiana and Bastrop in the northern part of the state. Together, the facilities produce roughly $1 billion worth of pellets annually for export to the U.K. Drax burns the pellets at a converted coal-fired power plant that supplies about 6% of the country’s electricity.

In Gloster, Mississippi, where Drax has operated the longest, several residents are suing the company over what they say is a decade of exposure to toxic chemicals.

“This bill uses taxpayer money to support a foreign industry and makes it easier for them to pollute Louisianians’ air and water,” said Naya Black, an organizer with the Dogwood Alliance, a group opposed to the wood pellet industry. “Biomass companies present themselves as clean energy companies, but in reality they cut down forests, process them into pellets and ship them overseas to be burned for European energy.”

The bill gives Louisiana Economic Development, a state agency, broad direction to draft new incentives for the industry. Drax has already avoided paying about $75 million in property taxes via the state’s Industrial Tax Exemption Program, known as ITEP, Verite News found in a review of estimates from LED.

Drax declined to address pollution concerns but thanked legislators for supporting the bill.

“We appreciate the engagement of lawmakers and our community partners in Louisiana,” a company spokesperson said in a statement. “We remain focused on operating responsibly and transparently, working constructively with regulators, and continuing to support jobs and economic activity in the communities where we operate across Louisiana.”

title: Green light for green energy: NSW moves to fast-track critical renewable projects - Dentons
description:
The NSW Government has introduced the Energy Legislation Amendment (Prioritising Renewable Energy) Bill 2026 (Bill), which would create a new framework for declaring and fast-tracking priority energy projects.
This alert summarises the key provisions, explains what the Bill means for renewable energy projects, and outlines the next steps as the Bill progresses through Parliament.
The Bill is designed to help NSW meet its energy transition targets by giving the Government tools to identify, prioritise and accelerate the delivery of the most critical energy projects.
Eligible energy projects include those involving transmission and distribution infrastructure, renewable energy generation, and energy storage or firming infrastructure (such as battery storage, gas-fired firming generation or pumped hydro).
The Energy Minister may recommend to the Planning Minister that a particular development be declared State significant infrastructure.
text:
The NSW Government has introduced the Energy Legislation Amendment (Prioritising Renewable Energy) Bill 2026 (Bill), which would create a new framework for declaring and fast-tracking priority energy projects.

This framework provides a key mechanism in enabling the Government to meet its energy transition ambitions, stemming from the Electricity Infrastructure Roadmap set in 2020. With coal stations wrapping up and increased electrification, there is a growing need for renewables to bridge the gap in tight timeframes- which fast-tracking can provide.

This alert summarises the key provisions, explains what the Bill means for renewable energy projects, and outlines the next steps as the Bill progresses through Parliament.

Introduction

On 6 May 2026, the NSW Government introduced the Bill into the Legislative Assembly - it passed the Legislative Assembly with an amendment on 28 May 2026. The Bill proposes changes to two key pieces of legislation (the Electricity Supply Act 1995 and the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979) to create a streamlined pathway for priority energy projects in NSW's energy transition.

What is the Government trying to achieve?

The Bill is designed to help NSW meet its energy transition targets by giving the Government tools to identify, prioritise and accelerate the delivery of the most critical energy projects.

In the accompanying ministerial media release, Minister for Climate Change and Energy, Penny Sharpe, emphasised the framework's role in fast-tracking projects:

"This new legislation will mean infrastructure projects that are critical for manufacturing jobs, economic growth and energy affordability don't get stuck in the queue."

Minister for Planning and Public Spaces, Paul Scully, situated the framework within the Government's broader efforts to improve planning system efficiency:

"With a growing pipeline of energy projects ahead of us, we need a planning system that can support achieving our ambitious energy targets," adding that since 2023, the Government has "already reduced assessment times for renewable energy projects by almost 20 per cent while delivering 50 per cent more approvals."

What you should know

The Bill introduces a new concept of a "priority energy project" (PEP). The Energy Minister will be empowered to declare, by written order, that a particular energy project (or a class of projects) is a PEP. The Minister may also appoint a person to make PEP declarations, provided they act in accordance with criteria set by the Minister. All orders must be published on the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water website.

Eligible energy projects include those involving transmission and distribution infrastructure, renewable energy generation, and energy storage or firming infrastructure (such as battery storage, gas-fired firming generation or pumped hydro). Notably, the Bill expressly excludes storage or firming infrastructure that requires coal-fired or nuclear energy generation.

Once a project is declared as a PEP, it may benefit from a streamlined planning pathway under the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979. Key features include:

The Planning Minister may declare a PEP to be State significant development without first obtaining and publishing advice from the Independent Planning Commission (IPC).

The IPC may, on request by the Planning Minister, hold a public hearing about development that includes a PEP. There is no right of merits appeal, for either applicants or objectors, against a decision of the IPC as consent authority on development that has been the subject of a public hearing.

The Energy Minister may recommend to the Planning Minister that a particular development be declared State significant infrastructure. There is also no right of merits appeal, for either applicants or objectors, on the determination of a State significant infrastructure project.

The Planning Minister may direct the IPC to exercise its functions at or within such times as are specified in the direction in relation to State significant development, State significant infrastructure or critical State significant infrastructure, including PEPs.

The newly established Development Coordination Authority is subject to the control and direction of the Planning Minister, except in relation to the content of advice, recommendations or reports it provides to the Minister.

Where a voluntary planning agreement is being entered into, the Minister may determine or direct another planning authority as to the amount of or method for determining the contribution to be made by the developer (involving land to be dedicated free of cost, a monetary contribution or other material public benefit) including by setting a minimum or maximum amount, or both.

Further Amendment

An amendment was agreed to in the Legislative Assembly on 27 May 2026, inserting a statutory review clause into the Bill.

The amendment requires the Minister to review the Energy Legislation Amendment (Prioritising Renewable Energy) Act 2026 and the Electricity Supply Act 1995 as soon as practicable after 12 months from commencement, to determine whether the policy objectives of the amendments remain valid and whether their terms remain appropriate for securing those objectives.

The review must also consider the quality of community engagement undertaken by proponents of priority energy projects, and whether community benefits arising from those projects have been allocated fairly and transparently — in particular, whether benefits have reached the communities most affected. A report on the outcome of the review must be tabled in each House of Parliament within 12 months after the end of the review period.

Next steps

The Bill has passed the Legislative Assembly and has been presented to the Legislative Council for concurrence.

What this means for you

Renewable energy developers with projects in the pipeline and their planners should monitor the progress of this Bill closely. If enacted, the PEP framework may offer a faster route to planning approval for eligible projects.

Do not hesitate to get in touch if you would like to understand how the Bill may impact you.

text:
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency hosted a 10-hour public hearing on proposed amendments to its coal ash cleanup requirements, which many speakers on Thursday said are gutting and a betrayal to communities nationwide.

More than 100 people testified against the new coal ash rules during Thursday’s online hearing, including various speakers from Indiana.

“The majority of Indiana’s coal ash is unlined and lying in the floodline of either Lake Michigan or one of our major rivers,” said Indra Frank, coal ash advisor for the Hoosier Environmental Council. “Indiana still generates about five million tons of coal ash per year. Given the heavy burden of coal ash in Indiana, (the state) will be hard hit by the proposed rule changes.”

On April 9, the EPA announced proposals to amend federal regulations focused on the disposal of coal ash in landfills and surface impoundments, according to the agency. Proposed rule changes would dismantle coal ash protections for operating and former coal power plants, exempt hundreds of coal ash dumps from regulation and permit owners of coal power plants to minimize, delay or avoid contamination cleanup, according to Earthjustice.

The EPA will accept public comments through June 12, according to its website.

According to Earthjustice, in 2015, the EPA established its first federal coal ash rule to require the closure of ash dumps and cleanups of leaking toxic sites. The EPA expanded its rule in 2024 to cover hundreds of “older, dirtier dumps that have been polluting for decades,” but cleanup of those has yet to begin.

Cecilia De Robertis, deputy division director for the EPA’s materials recovery and waste management division, said the amendments make changes to both coal ash rules.

“The EPA seeks input on the appropriateness, benefits and potential drawbacks of these provisions,” said De Robertis, who oversaw Thursday’s hearing.

Coal ash is a byproduct that is primarily created from burning coal in power plants, according to the EPA. It contains toxic heavy metals, including arsenic, boron, lithium, molybdenum and radium, which can interfere with child development and cause cancer.

Jenny Cassel, senior attorney for Earthjustice, said she’s worked to help protect communities from coal ash for about 15 years, and evidence of the harm “has piled up.”

“Water near coal ash dumps becomes thick with pollution, like a tea that is steeped for too long,” Cassel said. “Science — yes, that exists — has shown that exposure to coal ash is more dangerous than previously known.”

Climate change can also exacerbate coal ash threats, Cassel said, and natural disasters including hurricanes or floods can spill coal ash into rivers or other bodies of water, which can affect residents or those who clean up the coal ash.

“Many have lost their lives from ailments tied to the contaminants found in coal ash,” Cassel said. “Others who live near coal ash dumps continue to discover cancer at a rate that makes them think, ‘This can’t be normal.’”

EPA’s proposed changes would exempt coal combustion residual management units from the coal ash rule, and about half the coal ash that’s accumulated in Indiana are CCRMUs, Frank said during her testimony.

“The CCRMUs have already contaminated groundwater, and EPA’s proposed changes would leave them to continue contaminating groundwater and posing a threat in the floodplains,” Frank said.

Through the rule, Frank said the EPA will lower cleanup standards for nonexempted coal ash sites, which would allow more groundwater contamination and spill risk in Indiana. It would also allow coal ash to be stored in “unlined, uncovered piles for indefinite periods of time,” she said.

These practices, in Northwest Indiana, turned the Town of Pines into a superfund site, Frank said. The Town of Pines was contaminated by coal ash from a nearby landfill, which held more than one million tons of coal ash from NIPSCO’s Michigan City Generating Station.

The coal ash contaminated about 260 private wells and soil in dozens of the Town of Pines’ residential yards.

“People in that town are convinced that birth defects and cancers that they have suffered are due to drinking the contaminated water,” Frank said. “It is difficult to conceive why the EPA is proposing to allow practices like coal ash piles and fill, since those practices turned (the Town of) Pines into a superfund site. I implore you to abandon those changes.”

Cheryl Chapman, a Long Beach resident and member of the League of Women Voters of Indiana, testified against the EPA’s proposed changes to the coal ash rules. Indiana has 22 coal power plants with coal ash pits, Chapman said.

“Members across the state were so excited when both rules were adopted because it meant that residents could finally be assured that cleanups would make our communities safer,” Chapman said.

If coal ash seeps into Lake Michigan from its ponds, drinking water for millions in the Chicago area would be undrinkable, Chapman said.

“This is absolutely imperative for public safety and environmental health,” she added. “We anticipated that coal companies would fight against the 2024 rules as cleanups are expensive, but this is the price we must pay as a society. … We can’t evade this responsibility by changing the rules.”

Kelly Brown, water quality manager for White River Alliance in Indianapolis, said her organization “strongly opposes” the EPA’s proposed changes, saying they pose a significant risk to groundwater and surface water resources.

Brown told EPA representatives that groundwater monitoring and corrective action are important for communities nationwide.

“Coal ash contaminants are not isolated to groundwater,” Brown said. “Groundwater and surface water are interconnected systems. Contaminants can move between them in ways that threaten streams, rivers, drinking water sources and downstream communities.”

title: LG Energy Solution Shares Jump Up to 16% Following Major US Battery Storage Agreement
description:
DTE Energy has announced a substantial $1.6 billion procurement agreement with LG Energy Solution Vertech for the development and deployment of Michigan-made battery energy storage systems across the state.
The agreement encompasses eight distinct battery storage projects, which collectively will deliver 1.5 gigawatts (GW) or 6 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of capacity.
This includes the creation and support of an estimated 1,800 manufacturing jobs at LG Energy Solution's facility in Holland, Michigan, where the batteries will be produced.
From an industry-specific perspective, this collaboration marks a significant advancement for the energy storage sector and the broader clean energy transition.
For LG Energy Solution, the deal solidifies its position as a leader in the global energy storage market, particularly with its focus on expanding North American production.
text:
DTE Energy has announced a substantial $1.6 billion procurement agreement with LG Energy Solution Vertech for the development and deployment of Michigan-made battery energy storage systems across the state. This significant investment underscores DTE Energy's commitment to enhancing grid reliability, meeting clean energy mandates, and fostering economic growth within Michigan.

The agreement encompasses eight distinct battery storage projects, which collectively will deliver 1.5 gigawatts (GW) or 6 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of capacity. These systems are designed to store surplus electricity generated during periods of low demand and then release that power during peak consumption times. This mechanism is crucial for stabilizing the electrical grid, reducing strain, and minimizing the need to frequently start and stop traditional power generation sources. Deliveries of these battery systems are slated to occur over a two-year period.

A primary driver behind this initiative is DTE Energy's objective to comply with Michigan's Renewable Portfolio Standard and Clean Energy Standard requirements. Furthermore, the projects will support the escalating electricity demands from emerging data centers, including a notable project for Oracle in Saline Township.

The economic ramifications of this deal for Michigan are substantial. DTE Energy estimates that the agreement will generate a total economic impact of approximately 2.3 billion. This includes the creation and support of an estimated 1,800 manufacturing jobs at LG Energy Solution's facility in Holland, Michigan, where the batteries will be produced. Additionally, over 350 jobs are expected in construction and operations related to these projects. The emphasis on local manufacturing reinforces Michigan's role in advanced energy production and strengthens regional supply chains, building on DTE's prior investment of nearly 2.9 billion with Michigan-based businesses in 2025.

From an industry-specific perspective, this collaboration marks a significant advancement for the energy storage sector and the broader clean energy transition. It facilitates a more resilient and sustainable electric grid by enabling better integration of renewable energy sources. For LG Energy Solution, the deal solidifies its position as a leader in the global energy storage market, particularly with its focus on expanding North American production. While no direct geopolitical impacts are cited, the strong emphasis on "Michigan-made" and "US-made" components highlights a strategic move towards domestic energy independence and localized job creation within the United States.

title: Project cancelations are accelerating while developers compete for sunsetting clean energy ...
description:
The national, nonpartisan business group E2 released its Q1 analysis of large-scale clean energy project announcements, cancellations, closures, and downsizings since the passage of industry tax incentives in 2022.
“Federal policies designed to stifle clean energy are killing jobs, investments, and projects at an increasing rate.
Republican-held congressional districts are still seeing the highest number of both clean energy investment and project losses, E2 noted.
Texas is, perhaps unsurprisingly, still the dominant market for new clean energy development, with 10 new projects announced in Q1 2026.
The pace of new project development is still slower than the early days of clean energy policies in 2022, E2 noted.
text:
Clean energy developers announced 12 gigawatts (GW) and more than $19 billion worth of investments in the first quarter of this year, ahead of the expiration of some federal clean energy tax credits for solar and wind, but project cancellations also accelerated ‘sharply,’ according to new industry analysis.

The national, nonpartisan business group E2 released its Q1 analysis of large-scale clean energy project announcements, cancellations, closures, and downsizings since the passage of industry tax incentives in 2022. The updated tracking includes location, company, sector, and industry details for all announcements and project abandonments, along with the job, megawatt size, and investment totals from each project. As with previous monthly analyses, tables detailing project totals since 2022 by sector, industry, state, and congressional districts are also included.

How Much Clean Energy Has Been Canceled?

Overall, 45 projects, 41,000 jobs, and $14 billion in investments were canceled in Q1 2026. On the bright side, the 66 generation projects announced so far in Q1 are twice the total amount of projects announced in 2025 as a whole, per E2. The surge in new projects came as companies raced to begin construction before federal clean energy tax credits for solar and wind are phased out under recent federal policy changes from the Trump administration.

Project cancellations and downsizing continued to accelerate, as nearly 8 GW of generation capacity and more than $14 billion in planned investments were canceled, closed, or downsized through March. The number of projects canceled or downsized so far this year already represents more than half of all generation capacity losses recorded during the entirety of 2025.

“Developers are clearly rushing to get projects moving before federal tax credits expire, but the sharp rise in cancellations shows how much uncertainty is still hanging over the market,” assessed Michael Timberlake, E2 communications director. “Federal policies designed to stifle clean energy are killing jobs, investments, and projects at an increasing rate. What’s more, these mounting project cancellations mean we are losing badly needed new electricity sources that could power millions of homes and help reduce rising power bills.”

By the numbers

Electric vehicle (EV) and battery manufacturing remained the most volatile segment of the clean manufacturing sector, E2 said. Four of the seven manufacturing facilities canceled or downsized during Q1 2026 were related to EV or battery production. Since 2025, the EV and battery sector has seen 28 projects canceled, closed, or downsized.

However, grid and transmission equipment manufacturing remained the most resilient sector. With over $6.4 billion in active development across 58 projects, E2 tracked only one grid-related project cancellation since 2022.

Solar developments accounted for the most new announcements and cancellations in the generation space. Solar or solar-plus-storage projects represented 37 of the 54 new generation projects announced in Q1 2026, while 25 of the 38 canceled generation projects were solar-related.

Republican-held congressional districts are still seeing the highest number of both clean energy investment and project losses, E2 noted. Thirty-one of the 38 projects canceled in Q1 were in GOP-held districts, representing $10 billion in canceled investments. Democrat-led districts saw a $2.1 billion loss in investment.

Texas is, perhaps unsurprisingly, still the dominant market for new clean energy development, with 10 new projects announced in Q1 2026. The Lone Star state also saw 12 of the nation’s 38 canceled projects, including several of the nation’s largest canceled solar and storage developments.

Are the good times over?

The pace of new project development is still slower than the early days of clean energy policies in 2022, E2 noted. Between 2022 and 2024, developers announced more than 720 utility-scale generation and storage projects nationwide. Since the start of 2025, only 82 new projects have been announced.

Manufacturing investment also continued to slow in early 2026. Companies canceled or downsized roughly $1.4 billion in manufacturing projects during the quarter while announcing just $750 million in new investments — “far below the pace” seen in 2022 through 2024, E2 noted.

The previous E2 analysis covering the entirety of 2025 showed a drastic slowdown overall in the sector, tracking over $35 billion in clean energy project cancellations throughout the year, along with eliminating 38,000 current and future jobs.

title: NY's plan for nuclear power Upstate stirs painful history of pollution in Akwesasne
authors: Richard Haller, Richard Haller (News Intern), in Akwesasne
description:
New York State is moving forward with a plan to build a new nuclear power plant somewhere in Upstate New York.

He says he’s concerned with New York State’s potential plan to install a nuclear power plant near Akwesasne.
